title: Collection
summary: Collection is the tactic covering the adversary's staging of information of interest before exfiltration, including locating, gathering, and organising data from endpoints, file shares, mail systems, databases, and cloud storage. Behaviours include searching volumes and shares for keywords and file extensions, archiving and compressing selected files into a single staging container, capturing screen or clipboard content, collecting email from mailboxes, dumping database contents, copying data from software-as-a-service platforms into personal locations, and using built-in utilities to enumerate and read files at scale. This tactic is where defenders still have a reasonable chance of catching an intrusion before data leaves, because collection is usually noisy relative to normal user behaviour. Useful telemetry includes file access and creation events with volume metrics, archive utility execution and the size of what it produced, bulk download and share actions in cloud audit logs, mailbox export and delegated access events, and abnormal read patterns on file servers or databases. Detection in isolation is difficult because archiving and bulk reads are ordinary business activities for backup software, developers, finance teams, and administrators. What distinguishes malicious collection is concentration and mismatch: a single workstation compressing hundreds of documents it has never touched before, a service account reading an entire database schema, or a user downloading their whole mail archive shortly before resigning. Judging those cases requires peer-group baselines and business context as much as technical rules.
objectives: Describe how adversaries locate and stage data across endpoints, file shares, mail systems, databases, and cloud services.
Identify the telemetry that reveals collection, including file access volume, archive creation, mailbox export, and bulk download events.
Distinguish malicious staging from legitimate backup, development, and administrative behaviour using peer-group baselines.
Build detections that weight data volume and rarity of access over the mere existence of an archive utility.
Explain how data classification and least-privilege access reduce what collection can reach in the first place.
Connect a confirmed collection event to an exfiltration hypothesis and the evidence needed to test it.
